rationale: Both are real-world cohort studies of durvalumab consolidation after chemoradiotherapy in unresectable stage III NSCLC, evaluating the same intervention/comparator/outcome pairing (durvalumab consolidation vs none, PFS and OS). Stuschke's CRISP-registry cohort reports a significant PFS benefit and a favorable-but-not-statistically-significant OS trend across its whole durvalumab-treated population. Selke's single-center cohort, stratified by PD-L1 status, shows that benefit is not uniform: durvalumab significantly improved both OS and PFS specifically in PD-L1-positive patients (p=0.043, p=0.027), while PD-L1-negative patients showed no significant survival difference. Selke's subgroup finding qualifies Stuschke's whole-population result by identifying PD-L1 status as a likely driver of who benefits.

rationale: Dang's meta-analysis pools 28 randomized controlled trials (14,758 patients) and finds PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with chemotherapy improve overall survival versus chemotherapy alone in first-line advanced NSCLC. Katsarolis's independent real-world Greek cohort (610 patients eligible for outcome analysis) finds the same directional result outside the trial setting: immunotherapy at any line of treatment was associated with substantially longer OS than chemotherapy alone (17.5 vs 8.6 months; HR 0.51). An independent, non-overlapping real-world data source corroborating a pooled-RCT finding is direct support, not a restatement of the same data.

rationale: Nodbrant's Swedish registry study finds that lung cancer patients on palliative immune checkpoint inhibitor treatment with a good baseline ECOG performance status (0-1) have substantially longer median OS than those with worse baseline status (PS 2 or 3).
